newsitem.title: USA: U.S. economist says Fed should raise rates.
newsitem.headline: U.S. economist says Fed should raise rates.

text.p: An influential U.S. economist on Saturday said he saw a need for the Federal Reserve to raise short-term interest rates in order to prevent inflation from picking up.

Harvard University economist Martin Feldstein, president of the National Bureau of Economic Research, also predicted that the Fed will be hamstrung by political pressures and a lack of public support for higher rates.
"I think there is a strong case for increasing interest rates in order to prevent an increase in inflation," Feldstein told a monetary symposium here.
The symposium, sponsored by the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City, was attended by economists, government officials and central bankers from around the world.
Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan and a number of his colleagues from the interest-rate setting Federal Open Market Committee were present at the event.

At its most recent meeting on Aug. 20, the FOMC opted to leave interest rates steady despite concerns among some analysts that the economy might be growing quickly enough to spur inflationary pressures.

Feldstein pointed out that although the Fed is an independent entity, it is ultimately accountable to Congress, which created the U.S. central bank and has the ability to change its charter if it wishes.
Therefore, he said, the Fed is not completely isolated from political pressures, which right now tilt against higher rates.
"There is not public support," Feldstein said. "I think the Fed has to preserve its political capital."
Yet he predicted that the day would come when the case for tightening monetary policy to head off inflation will build.
"I hope that when it does come the Fed will act in a timely manner," Feldstein said.
